newsitem.title: JAPAN: TOKYO STOCKS END STRONGER WITH HELP FROM FUTURES.
newsitem.headline: TOKYO STOCKS END STRONGER WITH HELP FROM FUTURES.

text.p: Tokyo stocks regained their feet by the end of the Friday session with help from futures-linked trade in the afternoon, brokers said.
They said, however, that a wait-and-see mood hung heavily over the market ahead of the long weekend.
The key Nikkei 225 ended 166.20 points, or 0.81 percent, higher at 20,633,06. Its December futures finished 180 points up at 20,640.
"Futures buying emerged late in the afternoon, stimulating cash stocks and bringing up the Nikkei average," a trader at a second-tier brokerage said.

The benchmark was lifted in the morning by buying back after it posted hefty losses for two consecutive days. But in the afternoon, foreign investors' selling weighed heavily on the market as participants retreated to the sidelines.
The Nikkei average fell as low as 20,388.10 before futures-linked buying erased the earlier losses.

"Investment trusts which were expected to buy on Thursday, but didn't, bought shares today, boosting the Nikkei average above the 20,500 level near the end of the session," said Akishige Ishikura, Dai-ichi Securities analyst.

The U.S. payroll data due out later today, the formation of a new Japanese government and the U.S. presidential elections especially, both of which are scheduled for next week, were glueing most investors to the sidelines, brokers said.
They said they were worried about a possible shift in the current long-standing strong-dollar policy if President Bill Clinton is re-elected, which, in the long run, could hinder Tokyo share prices.
Market sources expect the Nikkei average to be basically stuck in a range of between 20,000 and 21,000 in the coming week.
Turnover was about 287 million shares, unchanged from the previous day, with advancing issues pulling slightly ahead of declining issues 552 to 517. There were 168 issues unchanged.

In other indices, the broader TOPIX was up 7.02 points, or 0.45 percent, at 1,557.57. The Nikkei 300 climbed 1.61 points or 0.55 percent at 292.05. The second section index however, shed 2.16 points or 0.11 percent to land at 2,030.77 with a turnover of 15.28 million, against 14.48 million on Thursday.
Foreign investors' selling especially hit steel makers, brokers said. Nippon Steel Corp settled one yen down at 331, the most heavily traded issue with 4.25 million shares.
Solid earnings lifted Mitsubishi Heavy Industries , which gained nine yen to end at 884 yen, the third most heavily traded issue on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
Matsushita Communication Industrial also rose on rosy earnings, jumping 80 yen to end at 3,090 yen.

Airline companies were higher due to lower crude oil prices, which means lower jet fuel costs, brokers said. Japan Airlines Co shares finished up 10 yen at 660 yen. All Nippon Airways Co Ltd was up four yen at 953 yen.
On a sector basis, the gainers were headed by railway/bus, oil, services, gas and real estate.
The losers were headed by sea transport, communications, securities and iron/steel.
